newsitem.title: UK: Sterling recovers above 2.80 marks in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Sterling recovers above 2.80 marks in Europe.

text.p: Sterling bounced higher to just below 2.81 marks by midday Europe after an early stumble to 11-day lows and should remain well supported by a buoyant economy and as long as EMU delay remains an issue, said analysts.
Sterling, which lost ground to the mark after France said it needed time to study the stability pact, was back on the attack, bolstered by a firmer dollar/mark and domestic fundamentals.
"Sterling is still in safe-haven territory," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN AMRO.
At 1115 GMT sterling/mark stood at 2.8045/55 against 2.7920/30 in late Europe on Monday.
Against the dollar, sterling stood at $1.6385/95 at midday against $1.6361/66 in late Europe on Monday.
But analysts said the foreign exchange markets overall are in a state of uncertainty in the wake of recent EMU developments.
They are looking for some clarification on the issue to emerge from a Franco-German summit scheduled for Friday and an EU summit to be held in Amsterdam next week.
"The FX markets, overall, are in a state of some confusion," said ABN AMRO's Norfield.
But with the latest set of UK data reflecting a healthy economy, analysts said the pound should remain buoyed in the short-term.

British retail sales, for instance, added spice to UK manufacturing data released on Monday which showed output was up 0.6 percent in April from the previous month and 2.3 percent higher year-on-year. Retail sales grew 4.8 percent year-on-year in May compared with upwardly-revised April growth rate of 4.1 percent, British Retail Consortium (BRC) said.
And further rate hikes are likely, unless the government tightens fiscal policy in its July budget.
The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) called on Tuesday for modest tax increases of up to two billion pounds in the new Labour government's first budget on July 2.
It said tax increases should be concentrated in the personal sector to dampen consumer demand, adding that there should be no net increase in taxes on business.
Kate Barker, CBI chief economist, warned that a budget that delivered no tax rises would lead to interest rates being forced above seven percent from the present 6.5 percent.
Peter Wood, trader at Bank of Boston, said sterling was likely to remain supported in the short-term as it was set to benefit from EMU jitters and perceptions of higher UK interest rates.
